  • States that Québec takes precedence over any incompatible rule, defines the Québec nation and its rights.
Part 2 Constitution of Québec
  • Includes personal rights and freedoms and language rights as fundamental rules.
  • Sets out the roles of the powers that make laws, govern, and judge in Québec.
  • Affirms values such as equality between women and men as founding principles.

  • Sets out Québec's role in choosing senators and Supreme Court judges.
Part 5 Act Respecting the Constitutional Council (new law)

  • Sets out how its members are appointed and how long their terms last.

  • Removes the rules on the former Legislative Council of Québec, which no longer exists.

Part 9 Executive Power Act
  • Provides that the premier chooses the person who will hold the position of Officer of Québec.

  • Specifies that rights and freedoms must be interpreted taking into account the collective rights of the Québec nation.
  • Provides that in case of conflict, equality between women and men takes precedence over freedom of religion.

  • Sets rules for requests to suspend the application of a law passed by the Parliament of Québec.
  • Prevents a court from raising on its own a question about the constitutional validity of a law.

• This bill streamlines the operating rules of professional orders and expands what certain health professionals can do.
  • It also changes the rules between pharmacists, manufacturers and pharmacy chains.
Part 1 Professional Code
  • Professional orders will be able to adopt certain regulations without the approval of the Office des professions or the government.
  • The Office des professions, which oversees professional orders, will now approve certain regulations, such as codes of ethics, instead of the government.
  • The Office will be able to decide which diplomas qualify someone for a permit or a specialist title, with the government's approval.
  • The Office will have to create a rule common to all orders to settle disagreements over professionals' bills.
  • The Office will be able to impose a rule that applies to one or more professional orders at the same time, after consulting those orders.
  • The Office will decide on its own the ethics rules for members of the boards of directors of orders, and will be able to investigate and punish breaches.
  • Professional orders will have to include more information in their official member list (the roll), and will be able to add other information.
  • The minimum number of signatures required to request a special general meeting of an order is changing.
  • People with a psychotherapist permit obtained elsewhere in Canada will be able to practise psychotherapy in Québec, under new rules.
Part 2 Act respecting nurses
  • Nurses will be able to initiate examinations and tests in more situations, not just in public health.
  • They will be able to prescribe examinations, medications, other substances, products and dressings, according to rules to be set later.
  • The rule that gave voting rights only to section delegates at general meetings is removed.
Part 3 Midwives Act
  • Midwives will be able to prescribe and provide more types of contraception.
  • They will be able to screen more broadly for sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections, and treat people without symptoms whose test is positive.
Part 4 Optometry Act
  • Optometrists will be able to prescribe and administer more medications and provide more care, with certain restrictions removed.
Part 5 Dietitians-nutritionists
  • Their scope of practice is updated, and they will be able to act without needing a doctor's prescription.
Part 6 Psychotherapy
  • The Interdisciplinary Advisory Council on the Practice of Psychotherapy ceases its activities.
  • Marriage and family therapists will be able to practise psychotherapy without a special permit, like psychologists and doctors.
  • The Office will be able to authorize students to carry out certain psychotherapist activities during their training.
Part 7 Agronomists Act
  • The definition of the agronomist profession no longer requires that an act be done for payment to count as practising the profession.
Part 8 Pharmacy Act
  • The government will be able to allow a pharmacist to prescribe or replace a medication with a product from a company in which they have a financial interest, under specific conditions.
Part 9 Act respecting prescription drug insurance
  • A new rule will allow a drug manufacturer to provide certain benefits to an intermediary, such as a banner or a pharmacy chain.
Part 10 Drug manufacturers and wholesalers
  • Manufacturers will also be able to provide these benefits to drug wholesalers, not just to banners.
Part 11 Several professional acts (agronomists, land surveyors, the Barreau, notaries, denturology, medical imaging technologists, etc.)
